=== FILE: Are You Secretly LOSING MUSCLE？ [-NEPgKfymHo].txt ===

  specificity is almost always at the top of the list. This principle states that the body will make specific adaptations to impose demands or will change accordingly to the style of training performed. The principle of specificity is a bit less commonly discussed in the context of hypertrophy compared to training for strength. In my view, specificity for hypertrophy is about how targeted the training stimulus is for a given muscle, specific region within that muscle, and theoretically even the composition of that muscle growth. Think things like fiber type specific hypertrophy. I like this definition for hypertrophy as it makes it clear that muscle growth is a seemingly local process. Back in the early 2000s, this topic was hotly debated in the research. To put this dispute into practical example, you may have heard that performing heavy squats in your training program improves muscle growth overall due to the systemic hormonal effects like increased testosterone that compound movements have on the body. This claim was put to the test in a series of studies out of the lab at McMaster University in Canada. First, a study by Wilkinson and colleagues demonstrated that muscle growth can occur in the absence of meaningful changes in systemic hormones that are often linked to anabolism. Then, a follow-up study by Weston colleagues showed that acute upregulation of anabolic signaling in the biceps were unaffected by systemic hormone levels that were manipulated by performing unilateral biceps curls with or without lower body training performed immediately after. Then, this same study had participants trained with these protocols for 15 weeks and demonstrated that muscle growth was unaffected by the systemic hormone levels. Ultimately, this line of research does a really solid job demonstrating how muscle growth seems to be a pretty local process in which a given tissue responds to the stimulus that's provided. And that brings us to the present study by Van Vossel and colleagues. The present study by Van Vossel and colleagues is part of an awesome large-scale data collection that has already produced a few cool studies. To briefly outline the project, 21 untrained participants performed a unilateral training program in which one limb performed lower volume and frequency training and the other performed higher volume and higher frequency training. For this paper, however, the results of the limbs were summed together such that each individual had a single data point contributing for each muscle group measured. The training program was focused on the upper and lower limb muscles, so the elbow flexor and extensors and the knee flexor and extensors, whereas other muscles like the calves were not trained. The authors measured the muscle volume via MRI of 30 muscles before and after the training program. Importantly, there were 10 primarily recruited muscles, 7 secondarily recruited muscles, and 13 non-recruited muscles. Participants were further separated after the fact into low and high energy intake groups to see if nutrition may have influenced the results between participants. To summarize the results, let's take a look at the main figure from the paper. You can see that the primary and secondarily recruited muscles all show significant positive changes in muscle size, which is intuitive. You grow what you train. However, the results of the non-recruited muscles is what stirred up the discussion. You can see multiple muscles that display negative changes in muscle size and even two muscles that reach statistical significance. To quote the conclusion section of the paper directly, to our knowledge, this is the first study documenting that some non-recruited muscles significantly atrophy during a period of resistance training. Our data therefore suggests muscle mass reallocation, i.e. the hypertrophy in the recruited muscles takes place at the expense of atrophy in non-recruited muscles, especially when energy and protein availability are limited. So the question is, do we really lose muscle to gain it? I personally don't think so, so let's break this down. This study provides an awesome example to discuss the concept of multiplicity. In traditional frequentist statistics, the common significance threshold is set as 0.05, which is also called the alpha level. The idea here is that over the long run, our risk of making a type 1 error, or what's called a false positive, is around 5%. The classic example for a type 1 error is telling someone who isn't pregnant that they are. This is a roughly 5% error rate is what we accept as a worthwhile trade-off in most fields of study. Now this assumption of a known type 1 error rate only applies when the assumptions of a given statistical test are abided by and only a single test is performed. When multiple tests are performed, the error rates compound in a way that isn't entirely intuitive. In the present study, while it's not entirely clear from the methods, I estimated somewhere between 116 and 174 statistical tests were performed, with no mention of a correction for multiple comparisons. To visualize what's happening here, I simulated what the expected type 1 error rate would be under these conditions, with a conservative estimate of 90 tests performed in the current study, which these are the tests that only directly apply to the individual muscle volumes. You can see as the number of comparisons rise, there's a logarithmic curve that is asymptotically approaching a 100% chance of making a type 1 error. For unadjusted comparisons, that's labeled in red. You can see at the intersection of the orange lines, I estimated the current study with a 99% chance of making a type 1 error. When applying a correction for multiple comparisons, you can see in the blue line, maintaining the desired type 1 error rate of 5%. To put simply, I don't really put much stock into the significant decreases in muscle size observed, or the correlations observed of energy or protein intake. The reality is, it's very likely just noise that is being picked up due to the number of tests that were performed. But we can take things a step further and look at this from a magnitude perspective as well. When I first saw the figure of non-recruited muscles that was getting a lot of buzz on social media, to me, it immediately stuck out as just a normal distribution clustered around a mean of zero. Here you can see a distribution of changes in muscle size from the current study in red, and a normal distribution simulated with a mean of zero and the exact same variance in blue. The point here is that the variability in the changes in muscle size are perfectly compatible with no changes in muscle whatsoever. I also plotted the mean differences of each of the non-recruited muscles with confidence intervals that were both adjusted and unadjusted for multiple comparisons. You can see that all but one of the muscles' confidence intervals now cross zero, which indicates no significant difference. And using some rough approximations of measurement error, all of the estimates are compatible with what I would personally call a trivial effect size. There are other things that I think could be further contributing to the excessive error rates, like pseudo-replication. Pseudo-replication is essentially when dependent observations, like 30 muscle volumes coming from the same participant, are considered independent. Here is a basic example that demonstrates how much of an influence this has on the precision of our estimates, and consequently the result of a significance test. From a practical perspective, I think this study does a good job in showing the difference between confirmatory and exploratory research. To be clear, I have no issues with the authors exploring the data in this manner to potentially uncover some interesting results that may warrant further investigation. But this needs to be factored into the way the data are interpreted. I've seen a few posts on social media that seem to make the case that this muscle relocation effect is definitely a thing, and discuss how this may influence our training. While I completely understand how that is enticing, hopefully this video goes to show you why I think that can be a bit misleading. When interpreting research, I think shot callers should be rewarded. Things like pre-registering your hypotheses, and statistical analyses prior to the data being collected, having a well-targeted research question, and attempting to achieve adequate statistical power for that research question, are the foundations of effective hypothesis testing. The best analogy I can think of is a dartboard. Imagine two different scenarios. In the first, you watch someone throw three darts at the board, one hits the bullseye, and two are very close. In the second, you watch someone throw 100 darts at the board. There are darts at every corner, and five hitting the bullseye. Who do you believe is a superior dart thrower? Chances are, you're going to value the first individual, as they demonstrated competency immediately with limited attempts, even though they actually got fewer darts on the bullseye. The same thing goes with hypothesis testing. Given the nature of error rates, we're bound to find some false positives some of the time, thinking something is there when it's not. This only gets worse as the number of comparisons are made increases, and thus, well-targeted hypotheses should be rewarded and viewed with more confidence. To wrap things up, while I think the muscle reallocation effect is an interesting idea that definitely warns in further investigation, I don't find the current study has particularly strong evidence to support it and potentially modify training based upon it. The reality is, with the number of statistical tests that were performed, it's more probable than not that a false positive is occurring somewhere, which in reality is just random noise occurring. Going back to the first study I mentioned by Wilkinson and colleagues, the Whitney participant's design had subjects only training one limb, while the other limb served as a non-training control. Significant growth was observed in the training limb, while no meaningful changes were observed in the control limb, and this would seem to go against the hypothesis of muscle reallocation, at least to some degree. If you want more free content like this directly in your inbox, sign up for our newsletter, which is the first link below. Thank you.

  a bit to just like some higher level principles about specificity and it kind of being something that you have reflected on not only in the strength data, but also in other data sets as well. So I'm curious your thoughts about just like high level principles about how it's impacted how you view programming and coaching. Yeah. And I think there are areas in practice that have been explored that haven't been explored in the research that just further shine that light to be the case even more. So whether you're looking at volume, frequency, proximity to failure, load, exercise selection, any of those variables, whether they're meta-analyzed or individual studies, whatever the kind of the highest tier level evidence that we have, I think every single one of those variables, if you think about it kind of on a principle-based perspective, kind of leans in favor of trying to essentially accumulate as many maximal force contractions as you can. So just briefly going one by one, you think about load. If you're training for a one rep max, the closer to a one rep max you're training with, those are going to be higher forces that you're ultimately producing, which are more similar to the maximal force one rep that you're performing for your strength assessment. For frequency, you're essentially saying, I want to split up the amount of work that I'm doing so that the performance for any given set that I'm doing is higher, which inherently comes with greater force production, which again is more in line. Volume, initially, obviously you have to do some contractions to be able to produce high force contractions, but after a certain point, that may start to take away to some degree in the short term, how many truly high force contractions you can do. If I'm doing a ton of training volume, that might in the short term not allow me to have as much performance under the curve. That may be offset by the fact that that has some positive effects, but in the short term, maybe that's not the best strategy. Approximative failure, if you put a given load on the bar, the closer to failure that you go, the more I'm going to be dropping my force production throughout that set. And that also probably has greater implications on the rest of my session and the rest of my training block in terms of the fatigue that may be accumulating, which is going to be less overall force production in that block. So you can basically pick out any single one of these training variables. And from my perspective, that's the story that comes out through dramatically. And then further, when you take all of those principles and put them in the real world, I think every single one of those is also coming through. And whether you look at Louie Simmons, we got a comment recently that someone mentioned that I didn't give enough love to Louie Simmons. Anyone that listens to the podcast regularly, I try to make it clear that Louie Simmons had a lot of these principles that we use from modern kind of strength programming down early with kind of a different way of application. But you have your heavy singles, your top sets from the max effort method. You have your kind of lower velocity loss back offsets from the dynamic effort method. The recent study by Mayon and colleagues utilized a simple cross-sectional study design. Various measures of muscle architecture were assessed in 16 trained and 13 untrained participants. The variable with potentially the most interesting findings was the estimated fiber number calculated by dividing the total muscle size by the average fiber size. The results of the study showed there was not only greater total muscle size in trained individuals, but also a greater estimated fiber number. The existing data on this concept seems to be much less clear. So does training cause hyperplasia? Let's dig into some of the basics of causal inference to address this question. Causality can be defined as the contribution of one event to the production of another event, where the cause is at least partially responsible for the effect, and the effect is at least partially dependent on the cause. In a simpler sense, I like to think about causality as the effect of having done otherwise, or observing what would happen in an identical scenario except for a single change. In the present study, the cause we're attempting to investigate is the effect of resistance training on muscle fiber number. We can symbolize this with the following graph. Now, in a cross-sectional experiment, there could be multiple confounding variables that bias the relationship we're attempting to investigate. One candidate could be the baseline fiber number of participants prior to training. The logic would go something like this. If an individual with higher number of baseline muscle fibers are more likely to seek out resistance training and stick with it, resistance training may purely be a form of selection bias rather than having a true causal effect on fiber number. This could be perceived as talent for the task, similar to heightened basketball in which tiler individuals are likely to seek out the sport independent of skill to some degree. Now, how much does this really impact our ability to detect signal from noise? The answer might surprise you, and here's a basic example with some simulated data. In this data set, I've simulated it such that we know there is no true relationship between X, training status, and Y, muscle fiber number. Without considering the influence of the confounding variable, this is what the estimated effect looks like. You can see a strong positive relationship suggesting that training is associated with an increase in myofiber number. Now, I've also simulated the confounding variable Z, which we can call baseline myofiber number, which has a very strong positive relationship with the myofiber number observed in the study. After we adjust for the influence of Z, which is baseline myofiber number, the relationship between X and Y disappears entirely, showing a slight negative relationship, which we know is closer to the true effect since I simulated the data. Now, the important thing here is that the confounding variables aren't just noise making the patterns we seek to detect weaker. They can entirely deceive us. So coming back to the study at hand, how do we interpret the findings? Without a hypothesized causal model that attempts to delineate all potential confounding variables, I view this study as mostly hypothesis generating for future work to investigate further. The findings are interesting, but we can't really conclude why they occurred with any sort of confidence. These situations are where randomized control trials are really helpful. They can help us isolate the causal effects very efficiently. If we go back to our causal graph, randomization allows us to eliminate all other causes of the independent variable, as it's entirely determined by the researchers, and thereby eliminates the bias introduced by the confounding variables. But the benefits of randomization can extend even further. They help to control against unknown confounding variables, which can bias observational studies even when a well-thought-out causal model is put forward. While there are limitations to cross-sectional studies and other observational research, I do think they get some unnecessary hate. The reality is the situations in which randomized control trials aren't feasible are still worth studying. One example is the impact of smoking on various health-related outcomes, and in that case, randomization would simply be unethical. Moreover, observational data sets often have a ton of benefits that RCTs, particularly in our field, typically lack. Massive sample sizes, ecologically valid conditions, and much longer study durations that actually look at the timelines that we're interested in the effects. Properly isolating causal effects is one of the most challenging, but also the most interesting aspects of research. Understanding some basic principles about causality and how data can deceive us in a variety of ways can make us all better consumers of information and allow us to apply research to our training more effectively. While the jury is still out with respect to hyperplasia and training, hopefully this video helped to walk through why the present study isn't particularly strong evidence of a causal effect between the two. === FILE: Exercise Variety is CRUCIAL to Optimize Muscle Growth [YXb05ekQgzc].txt ===

 nassin, nassin, nassin, nassin, nassin, nassin, nassin, nassin, nassin, nassin, nassin, nassin, nassin, nassin, nassin, nassin, nassin, nassin, nassin, nassin, nassin, nassin, nassin, nassin, nassin, nassin, nassin, nassin, nassin, nassin, nassin, nassin, nassin, nassin, nassin, nassin, nassin, nassin, nassin, nassin, nassin, nassin, nassin, nassin, nassin, nassin, nassin, nassin, nassin, nassin, nassin, nassin, nassin, nassin, nassin, n about the barbell back squat. Some will say the squat is the king of all exercises and it's all you really need to fully develop your lower body. However, if we closely examine the basic functions of the hamstrings, this claim gets a bit murky. The hamstrings are what are called a biarticular muscle, which just means they cross two joints, and in this case the knee and the hip. When they produce force, the hamstrings assist in flexing the knee and extending the hip. Crucially, in the concentric portion of a squat, we are simultaneously extending our knees and hips. These movements essentially cancel out the actions of the hamstrings, limiting its ability to contribute to the movement much at all. If we look at the longitudinal studies that have participants squat for some period of time and measure growth of the lower body musculature, we can see little to no hypertrophy of the hamstrings, supporting this idea that biarticular muscles may not be trained with movements that oppose their actions. The study used a within-participant unilateral design in which the right limb of each participant was randomized into one of four conditions, containing one exercise in the following two sets. For the quadriceps, we have the leg press and the knee extension, both performed unilaterally, and for the calves, we have the straight leg calf raise performed on a leg press or a seated calf raise machine. Each participant trained each exercise with four sets to momentary failure for each session, which was performed twice per week, with a target repetition range of 8 to 12 reps. The researchers measured the muscle size of five sites, the vastus lateralis, the rectus femoris, the gastrocnemius at both the medial and lateral heads, and the soleus. Now before we get to the results, I think it's important to describe what we'd expect if the squat and the hamstring example are generalizable. Because the rectus femoris and the gastrocnemius are biarticular muscles, we'd expect them to be better trained with movements that don't cancel out their functions. Thus, the rectus femoris would be expected to grow better with the knee extension and the gastrocnemius with a straight leg calf raise. When we take a closer look at the results, that's exactly what we see. For the rectus femoris, the knee extension condition had around a 99% probability of exceeding zero, while the straight leg calf raise had around a 90 to 99% probability of exceeding zero in the gastroc, depending on which head. Now these differences weren't huge, but for an eight-week study in recreationally trained individuals, the magnitude and the precision of the effects are notable in my opinion. The point here is that to optimize growth of the biarticular muscles, it's probably going to make sense to include exercises that allow them to contribute to the full success. I do think it's important to note that the other exercises did result in some growth. Thus, if you have limited equipment or really enjoy a certain exercise, you can still get a return on your investment and not all hope is lost. The other interesting part of this study is speculating why the monoarticular muscles seem to grow more in the opposite set of exercises. I wouldn't necessarily expect that. There are a few competing hypotheses in my mind. First, it could be that the resistance profiles of the exercises are potentially not controlled here. As an example, in my experience, the resistance profile of most leg press machines is the most challenging in the stretch position, whereas most leg extension machines are the opposite. Alternatively, it could be that the loading demands are spread across less tissue contributing to a given joint action, such that the training stimulus is more targeted or higher specificity in a sense. Finally, it could just be differences in absolute range of motion for each joint. In my experience, the amount of loaded knee extension I can get with a loaded leg press is far different than a typical leg extension machine. I'm sure there are other explanations. It's undoubtedly a combination of a few of them, but this trend does seem to be observed in the only other study I'm aware of that examines this concept. So it's food for thought. From a practical perspective, I think this study adds to the already solid evidence to suggest that exercise variety is a necessary part of program design to optimize hypertrophy. Specifically for biarticular muscles, exercises that don't train the muscle with conflicting joint actions are needed. As an example for the quads, you'll want a traditional squat pattern in an exercise targeted on the rectus femoris, like the leg extension, sissy squat, or reverse nordic curl. Exercise selection is a key part of program design. For optimizing muscle growth, accounting for some basic anatomy can make sure you're not accidentally leaving gains on the table unnecessarily. So any time the muscle was trained directly, that counts as one, one exposure. And if it's trained only indirectly, then that counts as half. There were three participants and they all did the same thing. It was just kind of a case series sort of thing. So it had to have multiple groups and folks had to be randomized to each group. Um, it had to train in a dynamic fashion. So if it was isometric training, it wouldn't be included. Um, and the intervention had to be at least four weeks long. Um, the study itself had to be the same in terms of every training variable, except for volume and or frequency. Um, and it's important to note that every single study had equated load and equated proximity to failure within reasonable bounds, because you can imagine scenarios where maybe a higher frequency condition could train with slightly heavier loads because they're less fatigued for some of those later sets. Right. Um, so we, we had some criteria for making sure those were reasonable bounds because in a lot of ways in a higher frequency condition, you want to allow them to train with. Um, you know, like slightly heavier loads or slightly more reps, um, because of that's kind of inherent benefit to, to frequency. But another way to think about it is we only included studies that should have compared volume and or frequency in a fair way. So everything else about the program was the same. Um, and then in the case of strength outcomes, it obviously had to measure strength and it had to be maximal strength. So if it estimated, um, wonder at max from velocity, something like that, it would not have been included. Um, so it had to use a maximal strength assessment. Um, if it used, um, like a dynamic traditional exercise, it could have been a one rep max. It could have been a five rep max. It could have been anything up to a 10 rep max. Okay. We also did look at isometric and isokinetic outcomes. Um, iso isometric, uh, strength assessments just mean you're basically pushing against an immovable object. Um, and the researchers can see how much force you're producing. And then isokinetic is similar in concept where you're looking at force production. Um, but it is against an implement at a fixed speed, um, which on one hand you could say, yeah, I'm a powerlifting coach. I don't really care about, uh, isometric or isokinetic outcomes, which is fair. Um, but we just wanted to kind of get everything we could, and we will have some figures at the end here where we just look at one rep max training, uh, to kind of confirm our main analysis does apply to, to powerlifting coaches. And then lastly, we did not include elderly subjects. So participants had to be, um, or no study could have been with participants older than, than 70. Anything dad? Cool. Um, but the, the TLDR of that is that we get this nice curve, right? We get a nice curve in terms of the independent effect of frequency on strength gains, but the analysis itself, the effect, uh, the effects themselves focus on within study between group effects, right? So as a, as a basic example, just because, um, my study used untrained participants and therefore saw really big strength gains because, um, you know, they have a lot of room to grow because they're untrained doesn't mean that the, the frequencies I used inherently get an advantage, right? So, um, it focuses on the fact that, Hey, all these studies are going to have inherent things that allow them to have more or less strength gain, but we're focusing on the within study effects between the two conditions, um, compared in, in terms of frequency. So we directly accounted for training status. So whether the participants were trained or untrained, um, we directly accounted for study duration, you would expect greater strength gains from a longer study. Um, and then we also directly accounted for the effects of volume. Um, so, um, if there is a direct advantage for volume, theoretically, our model would have been like, okay, um, this study had a benefit here and we need to kind of correct for that. And once you do all that good stuff in the statistical software, the, uh, the modeling process is basically looking at candidate models and giving and kind of ranking them, right? So specifically there were seven different model fits. For example, one of the model fits is a linear, uh, model where it's just Y equals MX plus B. And it kind of forces the data into that. Um, there are other ones as well and that are non-linear and considerably more complex. Um, for example, there were various spline models that could have indicated an inverted U if that was the best fit. Um, so anyway, there's, there's seven best model fits, um, or seven model fits. And then the computer tries to determine which of these best describes the underlying data, but also keeps things pretty simple or pretty reasonable, right? Because you kind of need to balance, Hey, what is actually a reasonable physiological effect and what describes the underlying data quite well here? Um, and then we also did a couple of other meta-analyses just to kind of confirm our main meta-analysis. So the main meta-analysis had 66 studies, which is quite good, but some of those were volume studies. And again, because of the methods we used, that should be no problem. But we also wanted to acknowledge stricter inclusion criteria where we only look at frequency, uh, studies, right? So we did two secondary meta-analyses to again, kind of confirm our main results. And we'll display those here in a little bit. Um, so the first of those two secondary analyses is a kind of a traditional contrast-based meta-analysis where you say, Hey, these groups trained with higher frequencies and these groups trained with lower frequencies. Where is kind of that pooled effect size in terms of higher versus lower frequencies? The second of the secondary analyses are probably better characterized as the tertiary analysis is, um, a two-stage meta-aggression, which basically creates an intercept and a slope for each study. Um, so let's say I have a, uh, a study comparing one versus three times per week frequency. Um, it's going to look at that effect, right? It's going to look at the difference in outcomes between one and three times per week, um, calculate a slope and an intercept for that study. And then those intercepts and slopes are meta-analyzed. So you can kind of get an overall slope. Um, and again, these two secondary analyses, the contrast-based meta-analysis and the two-stage meta-aggression are great for confirming directionality and to some degree, the magnitude and consistency of the effect in studies that only looked at the effects of frequency.  How did I take one of my clients, a very advanced lifter that's been training for 20 years from okay progress to adding 75 pounds on his total in just nine weeks? All right, today's video really comes down to what's called fatigue management. Let me explain. So, I'll start by saying that fatigue is a weird thing. In the research, fatigue is often defined as a decrease in performance below baseline. However, I honestly don't love this definition. So instead, I will define fatigue as any physical or psychological factors that take away from maximum strength capacity. Now, maximum strength capacity might be a little bit confusing. To wrap our heads around this, it might be helpful to think of a taper. So a taper or a temporary reduction in training stress pretty reliably increases strength. And this is why almost every power lifter does a taper in the one to two weeks before a competition. The reason a taper works is because there's basically always some fatigue present. And this fatigue takes away from expressing our quote unquote maximum strength capacity. Hopefully this visual helps. As you can see, normal productive training causes some fatigue. The dotted blue line represents a taper, which allows us to express our max strength capacity. However, this is just the start of the fatigue discussion. Fatigue exists on a spectrum, starting with this normal training fatigue, all the way to what's called overtraining syndrome. Between normal training fatigue and overtraining, we also have what's called overreaching. In my experience, overreaching is very misunderstood, but hopefully I can clear some of this up for you. I'll break this concept of overreaching into two categories. The first is overreaching with stagnation. The second is overreaching with regression. Let's start with the first. When experiencing overreaching with stagnation, we can potentially still recover to max performance capacity after a taper. However, there's a fine line here because overreaching can also cause regression. As you can see from the orange dotted line. As you can see from the orange dotted line. This overreaching is much harder to recover from. So put simply, if your training is leading to overreaching that causes regression, it probably is not worth it. Lastly, we have overtraining syndrome, which is characterized by sustained unrecoverable decreases in performance for months, often accompanied by negative physiological and psychological effects. Now it's been argued that true overtraining syndrome has never actually been reported in the research. So it's unlikely that this is something we need to fear in practice. Personally, I've never come across it with a client I've directly worked with. Nonetheless, overtraining would likely look like this on our handy figure. As you can see, performance not only decreases, but it's very hard to recover from it. Even after a taper. Now, I want to emphasize that this figure is conceptual and simplified. And there's some nuances it fails to account for. For example, it fails to account for some practical downstream factors that can come alongside training fatigue. These include factors such as aches and pains, disturbed mood, decreased motivation to train and disturbed sleep. Circling back to my client, Dustin, here's his data in the first couple blocks we did together. He's making some progress here, but it's not all that convincing. We actually did a taper at the end of this. We actually did a taper at the end of this, and he had a couple small PRs indicating to me that we weren't in that overreaching with regression zone, and we definitely weren't in the overtraining area. So I think he was somewhere between that normal training fatigue and overreaching with stagnation line. Now, here's where things get interesting. Dustin was presenting with some of those downstream factors that can come alongside training fatigue. The biggest one in his case being aches and pains. He wasn't necessarily injured, but these aches and pains were causing him to miss some sessions and also deload early. So we weren't able to apply the best stimulus that we could. We cracked the code, if you will, and Dustin hit PRs on all of the big three. So what did we do? Well, it came down to better managing fatigue. Specifically, we pulled back hard on his secondary days. And here's what that looked like. Some lifters or coaches may think these secondary days are not hard enough to progress. And while that might be the case on average, it clearly works for some. And when I take a step back, I think there's two reasons for this. First is that better fatigue management through some easier sessions meant less missed sessions and less deloads, which actually increased the total training workload when you zoom out over a longer time period. And secondly, this improved fatigue management meant feeling much stronger for his primary days for each of the main lifts. Dustin added 75 pounds to his PR total in a nine week period. And again, mind you, he's been training for 20 years. So hopefully you can tell that there's a delicate balance to be struck here. On one hand, fatigue is basically always going to be present with hard, productive training. On the other hand, if fatigue is too high, that will compromise the lifters ability to sustainably train with heavy enough loads or train with enough volume. All right, let's wrap up with some takeaways. First recognize that max strength capacity is often masked and it's masked by fatigue. But again, fatigue is a necessary byproduct of hard training. This is totally fine and expected. So long as you're avoiding training fatigue induced regression. Regression can occur for many reasons, including just bad programming or outside of gym factors. However, if regression seems to be occurring because of excessive training fatigue, you're probably overdoing it. Third periodize the degree of quote unquote, acceptable fatigue. If you're far out from competition or testing, you may be okay with more fatigue and slower top and strength improvements. Lastly, design training to protect your primary days. I like to tell my lifters that secondary and tertiary days may have a decent bit of fatigue going into them, but that's totally okay. However, training should be set up so the lifter feels good going into their primary day of the week, which again is typically the heaviest day. All right, that's the video. Please subscribe and check out the related videos somewhere on the screen here and we'll see you in the next one.

So, yeah, ultimately, when you're doing sets and reps in the gym, it's very common to have some sort of, like, set difficulty or exertion rating alongside that. My general approach before you play this, Zach, is just to kind of discuss what our general take on RPE versus RIR. My typical approach and suggestion for folks is to think of RPE simply as the inverse of reps in reserve. So, in other words, I actually almost exclusively use reps in reserve. However, there's a wrinkle to reps in reserve that we'll discuss where we like to use the term partials in reserve. And then there are times where we stray from that strict definition of RIR-based RPE. So, in other words, we do kind of use some other flavors of RPE in specific scenarios. Do you use a similar approach? Yeah. Yeah, I think so. It's just defining the task in different ways, yeah. Cool. So, typically, if you're thinking of RPE strictly in terms of the inverse of RIR, a 10 out of 10 would mean you have no reps in the tank. Either you complete a rep and you have no chance of another, or you actually fail the rep. A 9 RPE would be one rep in the tank. 8 RP would be two reps in the tank, et cetera. However, it's important to define what a rep is. And that's where partials in reserve comes in. So, in all of the power lifts, which is where a lot of this stuff originated, the hardest part of the movement is at the bottom. It's at the start of the movement. So, if you can't get another rep on bench press, it might come off your chest. And there are some people that fail at lockout. But generally speaking, the hardest part of the movement is at the bottom. For squat, same idea. You might be able to get a little bit of the way up, even halfway up at times. But you're not going to fail at the top, right? If you get through that sticking point, you're going to lock it out. Same idea with deadlift. Deadlift is a little bit more common to fail at lockout. But nonetheless, generally speaking, if you can only get a partial range of motion on squat, bench, or deadlift, you're not going to get another rep. Same idea with, like, a dumbbell bench press. Again, the hardest part is at the bottom. You're not going to get another rep. So, reps in reserve or RPE just makes a lot of sense for those movements because a rep is a rep. If you can't start the rep, you're not going to complete the rep. However, there are some movements where it's different. So, the example we'll show here in a second is a chest fly. Especially a machine chest fly. If you have it set up a certain way with cables, you can kind of change this and manipulate it. But for a machine chest fly, this is the case. For a leg extension, this is the case. For a lot of tricep movements, this is the case. A lot of lateral delt exercises, this is the case. A lot of back exercises, this is the case. Hamstring curls as well. Where the hardest part of the movement is not the start of the movement. It's the end of the movement. So, if you can't complete another rep at the very end of a chest fly where you're finishing the rep. Or the very top of a leg extension. Or the very top of a lateral raise. You do not have any full reps in reserve. But you absolutely still have partials in reserve. So, for a lot of those movements, because of the importance of approximative failure that we see generally in the research. And also some direct research directly on these sets where you go past that full range of motion failure. And you continue to get partial reps after that point. We instead will tell our lifters to think of it as partials in reserve. In the training session I did right before this, I did a couple of back movements. I did machine rows and I did lap pulldowns. On machine rows, once I could no longer get the full range of motion, I just squeezed out as much range of motion as I could on subsequent partials. For some exercises, you can get like 5, 6, 7 partials. It also depends on the rep range, of course. But generally speaking, 5, 6, 7 partials. Other times it's only 1 or 2. So sampling variance, I'll kind of go through these each quickly. Sampling variance is just the fact that let's say we have this overarching population that's in the clouds. This is kind of a, an assumption that we typically make, um, in research that we're trying to gain information about a population, but it's not easy to obtain all the participants or all the individuals that exist in that population. So we have to take a subset. So every time we take a subset, you're going to have some variability in the subset that you gather from that population. And so necessarily there's going to be some variability every time you take that subset. If we were able to get the entire population at once, there is no variability. We know what the population is going to tell us. And so when we have small sample research, the variance that we get from each one of these samples that we, that we have is going to be greater and greater and greater. And so even if we know what the population, you know, their, their mean is or, or whatever we're trying to calculate with a given study, the difference between two groups, even if we know what that is, because of the fact that we have small sample research, we're going to have a lot of variability that may lead some studies to find positive findings. Some studies that have negative findings purely because of the sampling variance and nothing to do with the underlying reality of the matter. And so that's the first thing to consider. The next one is measurement error. And that's something I think people have like an intuitive sense of is that even we have, you know, lab grade tools, we measure the exact same quality twice that we like assume to have the same true value.  I used to be pretty strict about creating a training plan and sticking to it, both for myself and my clients. However, I've changed my mind on this. If you stay tuned until the end, you'll see some example programming strategies that should help your results in the gym. What's going on? If you're new here, my name is Josh Pelland and I'm a strength and hypertrophy researcher. I also coach power lifters and other lifters interested in getting stronger and or more jacked. Today's video is about a shift in my perspective on how to manage a pretty foundational aspect of program design. Let me explain. So in the past, I was really bought into controlling everything I could so I could maximize what's called diagnostic clarity. Diagnostic clarity is simply the degree of confidence I have in evaluating what training variable or variables caused the training outcome or lack thereof. bench press and I wanted to bump it up to 15 sets, I'd previously only bump that volume up if we could logistically get it in every single week and really make sure we get those 15 sets in at the programmed RPE every week to ensure that I have maximum diagnostic clarity. In other words, I really valued and prioritized control over training variables so that I could try to tell what was going on and assign causality to strength or hypertrophy results. These days, this diagnostic clarity is less of the priority, at least for some lifters. And I think three things have contributed to this. The first is having less confidence in evaluating what quote unquote works. Honestly, I think coaches can convince themselves that they see a pattern for a given lifter that isn't actually there. Put more simply, it's really hard to truly know that a given client responds to X protocol and not Y protocol. This is a bit of a hot take. And if you're aware of our position on this, say three or four years ago, you know, this is a pretty big shift for us. It's largely informed by our research experience since then, and better understanding of variability and error. Put another way, given the error in measuring things like muscle size and strength, even in the lab with better equipment than we have in a coaching setting, it definitely humbles me in terms of the confidence we can have with a sample size of one with a given lifter that we're working with. Now, to be clear, I'm not saying we shouldn't still try to find what works for someone. Instead, we should be humble in our pursuit to finding what works and make sure it's not taking away from prioritizing training inputs, which ultimately drives the training response. This is the most important factor driving the shift in my perspective. If we return to the basic example of increasing bench volume from 10 sets to 15 sets, sure, we can try our best to differentiate the training response between the two volumes in a perfect world. And if we get the benefit of additional diagnostic clarity, great. However, if someone has a variable schedule, I'm going to prioritize getting the additional training inputs in, even if that means more variable training and thus lower diagnostic clarity. So some weeks Gibson may do over twice the total volume compared to other weeks. This is something that definitely decreases diagnostic clarity, but the benefit here is that we're prioritizing training inputs on weeks where he has the capacity to do so. Then it's my job as a coach to combine research informed principles and experience to best predict what he needs for future training phases. Now, you may be worried that some weeks will result in a decrease in volume from previous weeks, and you could make an argument that if you're used to a given volume, dropping the volume will result in ineffective training. However, that just doesn't seem to be the case, or at least if it is, it's not a massive deal. In fact, we have multiple studies in which the average volume goes down in the cohort, but meaningful hypertrophy still occurs. Put another way, just because you are doing 15 sets for a lift in one week, and then you have to do five sets the next week because of time constraints, that doesn't mean there's no chance of benefiting from the five sets you are able to get in. The final reason is a complete overhaul in our thinking on individualization. This is a topic that requires a lot of discussion, as well as some coming data from Zach's main PhD project.  alagin,自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由自由 gym, we should do that. We can benefit from time-saving strategies by either making the same progress in less time or making more progress in the same amount of time or some middle ground between those two. Today's video is all about supersets, specifically non-overlapping supersets. And we're going to answer the following questions. Number one, when to use supersets. Number two, how to execute supersets. Number three, we're going to give you an example split for hypertrophy training. I actually think this is the most slept on training split, if you will. And number four, an example training week for powerlifting focus. Before we dive in, let's roll our brand new intro. All right, let's kick things off by defining our terms here. So supersets are just exercises done in succession. Often people will use what's called antagonist supersets, which means opposing joint actions. For example, the biceps flex the elbow, whereas the triceps extend the elbow. For the most part, there isn't an inherent benefit to doing supersets with antagonist muscles besides the fact that they're non-overlapping muscles. In other words, the local muscular fatigue from bicep curls doesn't overlap with the local muscular fatigue from something like tricep extensions. So you could get the exact same benefit from doing supersets between, say, biceps and hamstrings, as those are also non-overlapping. The main reason someone would use non-overlapping supersets is in the potential time savings that come with it. Instead of just doing a set, resting for a couple minutes, and then doing your next set, you can just do two exercises more or less back to back. And this concept has been validated in the scientific literature to produce similar hypertrophy in less time. And it was most recently validated by Burke and colleagues, and they reported similar results with 36% less training time. So we know that supersets work, but let's dive a bit deeper and answer our first question of when to use supersets. Now, here's the thing to keep in mind about short rest period training, such as supersets. It can be really tough. In the case of the Burke study we mentioned before, the exercises used weren't the most fatiguing exercises in the world. They used pulldowns superset with Smith Machine Bench Press, leg curl superset with leg extension, and dumbbell bicep curl superset with cable tricep pushdown. Notice that there were no compound lower body lifts, such as squats or deadlifts, Romanian deadlifts, or even something like hack squats. Even without these heavy compound movements, the superset group experienced nausea almost twice as often as the traditional training group. The whole idea behind supersets is to do the non-overlapping exercise while the muscle you just trained is recovering. And this makes total sense, unless the reason you need the rest in the first place isn't because of that sort of local muscle recovery. Look, if you do a heavy set of squats, you're usually not stopping the set because of a ton of muscular fatigue, say in the quads. There will definitely be some, don't get me wrong, but there's a lot of muscles in the ballgame during a free weight squat, and you're going to be huffing and puffing at the end of that set. Usually, what allows you to do the next set of heavy squats is catching your breath and psychologically being ready to get after it again. So, to answer our question of when to use non-overlapping supersets, it's going to be when local muscular fatigue and not cardiovascular fatigue is what needs to recover. So, in general, smaller muscle groups and exercises that use less total muscle mass are going to be great candidates for supersets, whereas lower body compounds and sometimes even upper body compounds aren't going to be great candidates. That said, there's a lot of room for individual differences. If someone is in great cardiovascular shape, say they previously came from an endurance background, or they're just not quite as strong or muscular, and thus just inherently there isn't a ton of muscle mass being used, they may be able to superset even heavy squats with something else, because again, in that case, it's not cardiovascular fatigue that's limiting them and what kind of permits them to go into the next set. Next, we want to answer the question of how to execute supersets. Remember how the new study from Burke and colleagues reported more nausea? Well, I think that could have been avoided with just a small tweak. In the study, participants went directly from one exercise to the next. However, I would recommend doing supersets with a bit of rest between each exercise. So essentially what you're doing instead of in a single stage where essentially the computer is understanding the nesting, it's understanding the shrinkage, it's understanding all of these effects that, that that's giving us, we are going to manually do those steps. And again, what this is doing is it's removing the fact that these effects can talk to one another. It's removing the fact that all of the individual effects are going to be shrunk towards that population mean. They're going to be considered a distribution of effects with their own, um, true effect sizes. All that's kind of taken out the window. And what we're doing is for every single outcome, we are manually calculating the intercept and the slope for each one of those outcomes. And then we're going to, uh, pool those per study, which again, is that, that next level of nesting. So you're, you're calculating intercept and slope, um, per outcome, pooling those per study, and then ultimately meta analyzing the intercept and the slope to get those summary measurements of like a linear regression model that we can then make predictions from. So put a long story short, it's essentially removing all potential biases of between study information. You are calculating everything you would want to know from a dose response relationship, um, oriented model on the individual observation level, then pooling that per study, and then pooling that across studies, just like you would do with a traditional meta analysis, except now, now we're not looking at the between group effect size. We're looking at the intercept and the slope of a, of a, of a regression model. So y equals mx plus b. My hunch is that there's a relationship between our movement velocity early in a set and our perception of effort later in the set.
